speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade))
text: Competition spurs businesses to differentiate and innovate, so that they can become more efficient and productive.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade))
text: Consumers enjoy lower prices, wider choices and better products and services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade))
text: The economy also benefits as a result of greater productivity gains and a more efficient allocation of resources.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade))
text: The Act is administered by the Competition Commission of Singapore (CCS), which adopts a balanced approach in ensuring a robust competition regime that supports a level playing field for businesses in Singapore, without imposing excessive compliance costs or overly restrictive conditions on businesses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade))
text: With the aim of strengthening the current competition regime, CCS has reviewed the Competition Act to identify and address existing administrative gaps and to provide greater clarity on CCS' enforcement of the Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade))
text: As part of their review, CCS has studied the best practices and experiences of other foreign jurisdictions and engaged the relevant economic agencies and sector regulatory agencies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade))
text: CCS has also carried out a public consultation and most of the respondents have expressed support for the proposed amendments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade))
text: Some of their feedback has been incorporated into the finalisation of this Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade))
text: To start, I must explain that there are three main prohibitions under the Competition Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade))
text: This is a provision under section 34 of the Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade))
text: So, let us refer to this as the "section 34 prohibition".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade))
text: Lastly, this Act prohibits mergers or acquisitions that substantially lessen market competition and this is the "section 54 prohibition".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade))
text: During CCS' investigations into potential infringements under the Competition Act, an entity under investigation may come forward to voluntarily offer "commitments", or a pledge to undertake specific measures to remedy, mitigate or prevent the competition concerns which are currently being investigated.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade))
text: In accepting any commitments, CCS must be assured that the commitments are sufficient to address the competition concerns being investigated, can be promptly implemented and do not give rise to new competition concerns.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade))
text: Should CCS accept the offered commitments, CCS will cease their investigations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade))
text: Currently, only commitments offered for the section 54 prohibition are binding and enforceable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade))
text: In other words, if the merger parties breach any of the voluntary commitments previously offered to CCS, CCS will be able to take action against parties for the breach, without the need to re-open fresh investigations into the anti-competitive conduct.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade))
text: Clauses 5 and 6 amend sections 57 and 58 and are a consequence of the insertion of new sections 60A(1) and 60B(1).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade))
text: Entities may also approach CCS for a decision as to whether an agreement or conduct has infringed the prohibitions in section 34 or section 47.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade))
text: Clauses 2 and 3 are consequential amendments to sections 44 and 51, which allow CCS to make a decision that there has been no infringement if a commitment has been accepted by CCS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade))
text: This includes a commitment varied or substituted under section 60A(3).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade))
text: These amendments will align CCS' approach to commitments for all the three main prohibitions under the Act and also bring CCS' practices in line with other foreign jurisdictions, such as the United States and the European Union.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade))
text: CCS' current enforcement powers include the authority to require the production of specified documents or information and the authority to enter and search any premises.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade))
text: This is provided for under sections 63 to 65 of the Competition Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade))
text: Occupants of the premises being inspected or searched by CCS are currently required to only provide an explanation of the documents produced or seized on the premises or information uncovered during the inspection.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade))
text: CCS is not empowered to ask general questions in relation to the same investigation, without first serving a written notice, as provided for under section 63 of the Act, on the occupier of the premises or the individuals it wishes to interview.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade))
text: This limits the efficiency and effectiveness of CCS' investigations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade))
text: In addition, it results in confusion for the individuals being interviewed, as they may have to give their statement more than once and on the same issue as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade))
text: The occupier may also be puzzled as to why CCS has to serve two separate notices for the same investigation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade))
text: Clause 9 amends section 63 to empower CCS enforcement officers entering any premises for the purposes of an investigation to orally examine any individual on the premises.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade))
text: The amendment does not increase CCS' enforcement powers, but addresses an administrative gap in the investigation process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade))
text: CCS' scope of questioning is still limited to the subject matter and purpose of the investigation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade))
text: The proposed amendment also brings CCS' practices in line with these of the European Union.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade))
text: In addition, clauses 10 to 11 make technical amendments to sections 64 and 65 to provide further clarity on CCS' investigation powers, such as the power to require the production of a document at such a time and place and in such form and manner as may be required.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade))
text: As earlier mentioned, section 54 of the Competition Act prohibits mergers or acquisitions that substantially lessen market competition.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade))
text: However, not all mergers give rise to competition issues.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade))
text: Many mergers can preserve, or even enhance, the existing level of competition within the market.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade))
text: Singapore adopts a voluntary merger notification system, similar to Australia and the UK.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade))
text: This means that there is no obligation, or mandatory requirement, for entities considering mergers to notify their merger situations to CCS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade))
text: Entities who are interested to enter into a merger, but are concerned about whether the anticipated merger, if carried into effect, will infringe the Competition Act, may file a notification for CCS' formal decision; or in a situation where the information about the merger is not yet in the public domain, they can approach CCS for confidential advice.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade))
text: In the former instance, CCS will make their assessment and publicly release their decision on the anticipated merger.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade))
text: In the latter case, CCS' advice will only be released to the requesting parties.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade))
text: This approach is also consistent with practices in Australia and the United Kingdom, which operate voluntary notification regimes similar to Singapore's.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade))
text: Competition law is an important tool in ensuring that our markets work well, to encourage businesses to innovate and become more productive.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade))
text: This also brings about benefits for consumers as they gain faster access to a wider range of newer and better products and services.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Under the current Act, the Competition Commission of Singapore may, upon entering premises in pursuance to section 64 or 65 of the Act, require any person on the premises to produce documents relating to the investigation and provide an explanation of the said documents.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Beyond the ambit of sections 64 and 65 of the Act, where other information relating to the investigation is required, section 63 of the Act provides that the Commission may, by notice in writing to any person, require that person to produce to the Commission specified information relating to the investigation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The pursuit of higher efficiency in investigations has to be balanced against safeguards to ensure that due process is carried out.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I have some areas of concern which I would like to raise in relation to the proposed amendment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: First, given that the proposed changes have been introduced, taking into account the Commission's practical experience in enforcing the Act, would the Minister be able to share examples of how the need for service of the section 63 notice on the person to be examined at the premises entered into pursuant to section 64 or 65 of the Act has caused inefficiency in the investigation process or caused disruption to the businesses being investigated?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Third, under Regulation 20(3) of the Competition Regulations 2007, a person required by the Commission under section 63 of the Act to provide specified information or an explanation of a specified document in person may be accompanied by a professional legal adviser.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Fourth, under the proposed amendment, the investigating officers may require the individual being examined to answer any question relating to the investigation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: What safeguards are in place to ensure that the officers do not go beyond the allowed scope of examination?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Lastly, what safeguards are in place to ensure that the statements made by the person being examined are properly recorded, given that the Commission will rely on these recorded statements in deciding whether the Act has been infringed?

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I think it will be in order for all of us in the House to congratulate you on the arrival of your new child.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Deputy Speaker, I stand in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We must ensure that any corporate activity must keep the consumer in mind and not compromise consumer rights or positions.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Take the speculation of a deal between Uber and Grab in Southeast Asia, for instance.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Will it achieve a dominance that will crowd out other taxi companies?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Hence, our competition laws must be robust to ensure that corporate activities do not create anti-competitiveness or undermine our market fundamentals.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: As such, the Competition Bill will strengthen the CCS as a key guardian of our consumers' interest.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I welcome the expanded scope of enforcement for CCS that this Bill allows.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: At the same time, the move to allow CCS to provide confidential and non-binding advice is also a positive step.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: At this juncture, I hope the Government can provide an update on the focus of CCS in the past few years.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: How many instances of corporate activities did it evaluate and how often did it act on these corporate activities?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I would also like to further suggest that CCS keep a strong focus on looking at corporate activities in companies engaging in essential services and services that touch the lives of Singaporeans daily.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: This will ensure that corporate activities do not negatively impact Singaporeans' general cost of living.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: On a separate note, I hope the Government can consider setting up a committee that will look at profiteering, especially of essential services.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The committee can also take on feedback and tip-offs from consumers.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: While the instance of profiteering may be few and far between in Singapore, the mere existence of such a committee will serve as a deterrence to unscrupulous merchants.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: First, the onset of competition and its merits and demerits; and, secondly, the concerns on the proposed amendments, namely, section 60A(1A) and 60A(1B).

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: First, let me cover the onset of competition and its merits and demerits.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore professes and practises an open economy and its market is more or less driven by market forces.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: It is believed that an open market with healthy competition will lead to competitive prices offered to consumers.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: A healthy competition would also weed out the non-performers.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Non-productive and non-competitive business players and retailers will automatically be driven out of the marketplace.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: New players will emerge and offer a more competitive product.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Like the law of the jungle, the survival of the fittest seems to be the rule of the day.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Thus, overall, the outcome should benefit the consumer and prices offered will reach its optimum and settle to an equilibrium that is low enough for consumers to benefit and high enough for business owners and retailers to profit.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: It is an ideal case where competition is doing its job.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: While we can see this from the consumer standpoint, which is positive as the consumer stands to benefit from this scenario, there also lies the dark side to this so-called healthy competition.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Open competition has resulted in many traditional and typical mom and pop retail shops being squeezed out of their traditional home-ground, that is, the heartlands, with the influx of retail giants into the heartlands.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: This has caused a lot of unhappiness with small business owners.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: While open competition has taken its natural course, its impact can be devastating for some whose income may solely depend on this traditional business.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Just like when we have an Act to protect and preserve some old buildings and monuments, we might want to do the same for some of our traditional businesses.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I am certain that we will be able to strike a balance between keeping our traditional businesses afloat and opening our market towards open competition.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Apart from the traditional and typical neighbourhood retailers, our small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) are also facing stiff competition from global overseas players.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: This is inevitable as we have an open market which is riding on the global economy.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: While there are merits to this chosen framework, the impact on the local scene is devastating for some.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Again, the survival of the fittest will weed out the smaller players.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: More often than not, our SMEs and small business retailers will be the victims of such an onslaught.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: It is imperative that our SMEs are protected, as they play a key role in our nation’s economic growth.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: While we advocate and practise open competition, we must be mindful of the impact it may bring if it brings along with it a negative impact which is detrimental to our nation’s economy.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: While I am not against open competition, which can be healthy, we should and must try to give some level of assurance to our SMEs and small retailers that due consideration is given to them in this competitive environment.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: This delicate situation needs to be intelligently considered, as we would also like our SMEs to be able to benefit from the global market.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Vice versa, our SMEs will automatically be faced with competition at home from overseas competitors, as reciprocity is expected if we are to be given the opportunity to explore overseas markets.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I hope the relevant Ministry will be able to consider this suggestion.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Expansion and collapse of business entities are left very much to market forces and individual business decisions.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: While there could be instances of bailout situations, perhaps due to extreme and detrimental cases, more or less, private business entities decide on their course of action.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Mergers and acquisitions (M&A) may be one of the inorganic growth strategies undertaken by private business entities in trying to expand their business in the market.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: However, if left unchecked and unmonitored, the impact of M & As can be detrimental.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Having gone through personally three M&A events during my career, I have witnessed both the upside and downside of an M&A.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: While it is expected to bring positive end results for business in an M&A, more often than not, the downside will be on the restructuring process which will most probably result in manpower redundancy.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: More worrying is the impact to the market after an M&A on competition.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Will the result of a particular M&A make the competition healthier which results in a better situation for the customers and end consumers?

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: If yes, then it is deemed as a good M&A.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: My question is: does this mean that the Commission can still decide that the merger is prohibited under section 57 after giving advice to the contrary earlier?

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Take note section 57 states that a party to an anticipated merger must notify the Commission and apply to it for a decision.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: The Commission will then decide if such a merger is lawful.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: And also note the difference between an advice under section 55A and the decision under section 57.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Currently, the Commission may only require companies to undertake commitments for the prohibitions under section 54.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Ministry shed some light on this matter?

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Healthy competition is expected to benefit consumers by and large.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: As mentioned earlier, the outcome of healthy competition should reach an optimum offer to consumers and settle to an equilibrium: low enough for consumers to benefit and enough for business owners and retailers to profit.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: It is an ideal case where competition is doing its job.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, it is imperative that we should strive to achieve a healthy competition scenario, striking a balance between an open and free market economy against a regimented one.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Like many situations, an acceptable and optimum condition can only be achieved if the surrounding parameters are monitored and managed.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: With that, Mr Deputy Speaker, notwithstanding the comments and suggestions I have made, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that this seeks to codify an already available procedure.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Statutory force is likely to further assure businesses approaching the Commission for such advice that such an approach will be treated on a confidential basis.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The one aspect of the proposed amendments that is of concern is the powers of persons entering into premises with or without a warrant for the purpose of investigations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Currently, investigating officers, inspectors and other authorised persons may enter into premises with or without a warrant for the purpose of carrying out investigations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Persons on the premises can be required to: (a) Produce documents relating to any matter relevant to the investigatons; (b) Provide an explanation of that document, if it is so produced; and (c) State to the best of his knowledge where any such document is found.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These are specific questions relating to documents relevant to the investigations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If the Commission or Inspector wishes to ask other questions on matters relevant to the investigation, the person must be served with a notice in writing under section 63.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My concern is that notices will never be served on persons found on premises when they are questioned on relevant matters beyond documents relating to the investigation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The requirement for notice allows time for a person required to act under it to consider the request made and perhaps seek legal advice on it.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Senior Minister of State clarify again why we are making this amendment and perhaps why did we have this requirement for serving a notice in the first place?

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Some have raised pertinent points that I will now address.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Azmoon Ahmad asked if the proposed amendment to allow CCS to accept legally-binding commitments for cases involving the section 34 and section 47 prohibitions makes it easier for companies to circumvent competition law.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And in assessing their acceptance of commitments, CCS must also be assured that the commitments are sufficient to prevent the recurrence of such anti-competitive conduct.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The proposed amendment allows CCS to take more timely action against a party, which had previously provided but breached a commitment, so they do not then need to re-open fresh investigations into the anti-competitive conduct itself.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This strengthens, rather than limits, CCS' enforcement efforts to eliminate and control anti-competitive practices in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Patrick Tay has asked about how the need for the service of the section 63 notice on the person to be examined during CCS' inspections and searches conducted pursuant to sections 64 and 65 of the Competition Act has resulted in an inefficient investigation process or caused disruption to the business being investigated.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In addition, Mr Tay has asked about the safeguards to ensure that the person examined is sufficiently informed of the subject matter and purposes of the investigation.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The notice or warrant issued pursuant to sections 64 or 65 of the Competition Act respectively, allows CCS to obtain documents relating to the investigation and require any person to provide an explanation of these documents, including where to locate the documents if they are not on the premises.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Prior to entering the premises, CCS has to serve the section 64 notice or section 65 warrant on the occupier of the premises.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This notice or warrant states the subject matter and the purpose of CCS’ investigation, which will be explained to the occupier as well.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: CCS will also make clear the occupier’s and the occupants' obligations and rights, such as it being an offence if they provide false or misleading information to the investigating officer.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: However, CCS may, sometimes, need to also ask general questions that are related to the subject matter and purpose of the investigation, but which do not relate to the explanation of the documents obtained at that point in time.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For example, without the proposed amendments, if the scope of CCS' investigations is on bid-rigging and CCS uncovers an email correspondence chain relating to the rigging of a tender during an inspection, they would only be able to require any person to explain what the email correspondence is about, but would not be able to ask about what other related projects the parties in the email may also have been involved in.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, it could well be many, many bid-rigging episodes but the email documented one episode and, without this broader scope of questioning, they are limited in only being able to obtain that information about that one episode.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For CCS to be able to do more than that, it would need to first serve a separate section 63 notice on the individual they wish to examine and re-explain the necessary obligations and rights to the individual again – a redundant duplication of work, both for the agency and for the individual.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This prolongs the duration of the inspection or search and results in a longer than necessary disruption to the business being investigated.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It also results in two separate statements being recorded from the same person, one pursuant to the powers under section 63 and the other under section 64.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Patrick Tay also asked whether a person being examined would be allowed access to legal representation, about the safeguards that the statements are properly recorded and that CCS officers do not go beyond the allowed scope of questioning.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Louis Ng also raised a concern about the individual having sufficient time to seek legal advice on CCS’ requirements.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In addition, where a written notice is addressed to an individual, it is not acceptable for another person to respond on that individual’s behalf.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But this does not prevent the individual from obtaining legal advice in relation to that notice.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As a further safeguard, the subject matter and purpose of the investigation are also stated in the notice or warrant issued pursuant to sections 64 and 65 of the Act, which CCS officers strictly adhere to.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Hence, they will only ask questions related to the subject matter.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Furthermore, the statement given by the individual has to be read to the individual in a language he understands, before he signs the statement.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The individual also has the opportunity to correct the statement, if necessary.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In addition, should CCS rely on the statement for their decision, CCS will first issue a Proposed Infringement Decision (PID).

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Parties will be able to inspect CCS' evidence and make representations to CCS, including if they feel that CCS has gone beyond the scope of investigations during the interview, in response to the PID.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: CCS will take into consideration parties' representations, before issuing their final decision in an Infringement Decision or ID.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: If parties disagree with CCS' decision in the ID, they may appeal to the Competition Appeal Board, which is an independent body, comprising members appointed by the Minister for Trade and Industry.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The introduction of new section 55A formalises CCS' provision of confidential advice on anticipated mergers in the situation where information about the merger is not yet in the public domain.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In the spirit of confidentiality, therefore, CCS will base its assessment of the anticipated merger on the information provided by the merging entities.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: CCS will not request for information from any third party, such as the applicant's main customers or competitors, or conduct any public consultation to assist in their assessment because it is meant to be confidential advice.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In the situation where information about an anticipated merger is already in the public domain, merging entities may make an application for CCS' formal assessment of whether the anticipated merger, if carried into effect, will infringe the section 54 prohibition.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This is provided for under section 57 of the Competition Act.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This is provided for under the existing section 59 of the Act.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Henry Kwek asked whether the speculated merger between Uber and Grab will achieve a dominance that will crowd out other taxi companies, causing consumers to ultimately lose out.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: CCS has the power to review any merger which may result in a substantial lessening of competition in any market in Singapore and is monitoring this matter.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Henry Kwek also asked for an update on CCS' focus over the past few years.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: CCS continues their efforts to ensure effective enforcement of the Competition Act and to raise awareness of competition law in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This includes their work in assessing merger notifications and conducting market inquiries, in order to ensure that markets work well for both businesses and consumers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Over the past five years from 2013 to 2017, CCS has investigated into nearly a hundred cases of potential infringements of the Competition Act.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I also note Mr Henry Kwek's feedback on asking the Government to consider setting up a committee to look into profiteering.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In addition, Mr Azmoon Ahmad has suggested for the Government to take into consideration, in our future reviews of the Competition Act, the need to protect our traditional businesses, as well as our SMEs.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The Government notes the feedback and I also wish to clarify that the Competition Act is a broad-based legislation targeted at promoting efficient market conduct to protect consumers and businesses from anti-competitive activities.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In this regard, there may be more targeted ways to help our SMEs, such as through the support given by our various economic agencies.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The proposed amendments seek to address existing administrative gaps, in order to strengthen the current competition regime.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Competition law is an important tool to ensure well-functioning and healthy markets, to ensure a level playing field for all businesses to compete and innovate, such that they can become more efficient and productive, which is essential for Singapore's next phase of innovation-driven economic growth.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: With that, Mr Deputy Speaker, I beg to move.      .
